newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia '97 budget to target high-quality growth.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia '97 budget to target high-quality growth.

text.p: After applying the brakes to curb surging growth last year, Malaysia is likely in its 1997 budget to focus on raising production, home-grown manufacturing, high-technology and savings, analysts said.

Measures announced in the 1996 budget included efforts to stem consumer spending by raising minimum monthly credit card payments, raising road tax on luxury cars and imposing a 100,000 ringgit ($40,000) levy on foreigners buying real estate.

But, the economy -- while still in its ninth year of more than eight percent expansion -- has slowed since last year's 9.6 percent clip. Gross domestic product (GDP) grew at 8.4 percent in the second quarter of 1996.
"There is much less need to focus on an overheating economy," said P.K. Basu, regional economist at UBS Securities. "I think this (budget) will be less restrictive than the last one."

Overall, no big surprises are expected in the budget, set to be tabled in parliament on October 25 by Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim. Economists say next year's economic blueprint will be boring, but benevolent to financial markets.

One possible boost is from an expected one to two percent cut in the corporate tax rate from 30 percent to keep Malaysia competitive with its neighbours. Rates are as low as 26 percent in Singapore, economists said.
Much of what is forecast to be in the budget has already been hinted at in Malaysia's most recent five-year blueprint.

"As clearly spelled out in the 7th Malaysia Plan, the government will opt for a productivity-driven growth path with more emphasis on information technology, skill upgrading, capital deepening and technological development and less on input-driven growth," a report from O.S.K. Research said.
While Malaysia's troublesome balance of payments deficit has improved, analysts say the new budget is likely to still stay the course on narrowing the current account deficit.

The account deficit ballooned to 17.8 billion ringgit in 1995 from 10.9 billion the previous year. The government has said that should fall to 17 billion this year, but economists are even more bullish, estimating a gap of 14-15 billion.

"For the first time in three years, I'm not expecting anything drastically negative," said Rajeev Malik, senior economist at Jardine Fleming, referring to the budget. "We've just come out of an overheating phase. It's a totally different phase in the cycle."

Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad has already said the budget will focus on reducing unnecessary imports. The purchase of heavy equipment in Malaysia's rush to industrialise put a heavy toll on its foreign expenditures.

Jupiter Securities said in a report that it expects a liberalisation of export duties, particularly in electrical and electronic items -- already Malaysia's biggest earners -- as well as "expanding incentives to encourage the promotion of Malaysian brand names".

Fresh from last August's promotion of its Multimedia Super Corridor (MSC), which aims to create an information technology hub, Malaysia is also expected to stress the importance of high-technology, analysts said.
"The major area the government is looking at is a shift towards high-tech, high-value-added investments," said an economist at a local research house.

Boosting tourism and other service industries will also be a priority, analysts said. "Tourism was the top foreign exchange earner, with a net inflow of $5 billion ringgit last year," said Vickers Ballas in its budget assessment.
Savings will be promoted, economists said. PhileoAllied Securities said in a report that the government aims to raise the 34.3 percent savings rate to 40 percent.
"We may see separate tax relief allowed for contributions to approved pension funds," it said.
